facts.claim: The single "Doubt" by The Bridge City Sinners was released May 10, 2024, with a copyright line to Flail Records. It runs 2:36.
"Doubt" appears on the album In the Age of Doubt, released July 12, 2024 on Flail Records and SBÄM Records.
The distributor metadata for the "Doubt" single credits Kristofer (Kris) Crummett as producer.

On the parent album, Kris Crummett produced, engineered, mixed and mastered at Interlace Audio in Portland, OR. Joseph Faison IV did additional production, and the horns were engineered by Stephan Hawkes in Los Angeles. The Bandcamp credits say all songs were written by the Bridge City Sinners.

The album's band lineup is Libby Lux (lead vocals, banjolele), Michael Sinner (resonator guitar, vocals), Lightnin' Luke (violin, piano, vocals), Clyde McGee (banjo, vocals) and Scott Michaud (upright bass, vocals). Additional musicians include Charles De Castro on trumpet on several tracks.
Lead singer Libby Lux said the song speaks to the battle within and how you are your own worst enemy. She called it a reminder not to give in to thoughts of self-harm and self-hatred.

The band says In the Age of Doubt follows the sonic direction of Unholy Hymns, combining folk instrumentation with heavier, more alternative styles. It is set in the same fictional, hedonistic, post-apocalyptic world as Unholy Hymns.
Flail Records was started by the Sinners and is run by bassist Scott Michaud.
Bridge City Sinners are a Portland, Oregon band. They began as buskers in the Pacific Northwest, and the band describes its range as running from Prohibition-era jazz to Appalachian death folk.
The band's earlier releases are Bridge City Sinners (2016), Witches' Wrath (2018), Here's to the Devil (2019) and Unholy Hymns (2021). Unholy Hymns entered the Billboard charts at number 70.

research.lineage: The band sits in a dark folk / dark Americana string-band tradition, with roots in Pacific Northwest busking and a punk-scene DIY ethos, blending Appalachian death folk, prohibition-era jazz and heavier alternative sounds.

draft:
The upright bass on **Doubt** walks like it has somewhere to be. A plucked line moves under a steady drum kit with a loose swing, a banjo chops out the rhythm, and a fiddle draws a melody heavy with vibrato over the top. It's a band playing at a dancing tempo, not a funeral pace. That matters, because the song is about the voice in your own head that wants you gone.

Libby Lux, the Bridge City Sinners' lead singer, has said the song speaks to the battle within, the sense that you are your own worst enemy. She framed it as a warning against giving in to thoughts of self-harm and self-hatred. That's a heavy thing to carry, and the band doesn't slow down to carry it. The groove keeps pushing forward. That choice reads as its own kind of answer. When the doubt gets loud, you keep your feet moving, keep playing, and stay in the room with the people playing beside you.

The single voice out front is clear and resonant, sung with real expression and no harmonies to lean on. Alone like that, it sounds exposed in a way that suits a song about fighting yourself, because nobody else can step into that argument. The production lets the room in. It's open and natural, raw and unpolished, and the strings sound played rather than sanded smooth.

That rawness has a history. The Sinners started out busking in the Pacific Northwest, and they describe their range as running from Prohibition-era jazz to Appalachian death folk. You can hear both ends here, in the swing of the rhythm section and the mountain bite of fiddle and banjo. On record, that's Lightnin' Luke on violin, Clyde McGee on banjo, and Scott Michaud on upright bass. Michaud also runs Flail Records, the label the band started themselves, and that do-it-yourself streak runs through the sound.

Their 2021 album Unholy Hymns pushed folk instrumentation toward heavier, more alternative styles, and it entered the Billboard charts at number 70. The band says the new album, In the Age of Doubt, follows the same path and returns to the same fictional, hedonistic, post-apocalyptic setting. The record takes its name from this song's single word, and the logic holds. When everything outside has burned down to excess, the enemy that's left is the one inside. Kris Crummett produced in Portland at Interlace Audio, and he keeps the band close and unvarnished. Every song on the album is credited to the group as a whole, which fits a track that sounds like five people holding a line together.

**Doubt** takes the loneliest fight a person has and sets it to a rhythm you can't help moving to, so you come away feeling that the self-hatred is real, and that you don't have to stand still for it.
